conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the surgery team. I understand you’ve had worsening abdominal pain for about three days, mostly around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sharp constant pain right where the tube is. My belly also feels really full. It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, chills, redness, drainage, or pus around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. It looks the same. Just hurts a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any vomiting, blood in stool, black stools, or not passing gas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bleeding. I’m passing gas and I’ve had bowel movements. I do get nauseated sometimes, but mostly it’s pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you doing with tube feeds at home? Did you try holding them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t hold them. If I stop, my sugar drops fast. But when I run feeds, the pain feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense given your history of hypoglycemia. Our first priority is keeping your blood sugar safe while we figure out the pain. We’ll check fingerstick sugars regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared you’re going to tell me it’s all in my head again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Your pain is real. The question is what’s driving it—tube site irritation, abdominal wall pain, stomach irritation, or something else. We’ll take it step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam, I don’t see signs of infection at the tube site—no redness, swelling, or drainage. Your belly is soft, and the tenderness is mostly around the tube and left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens tonight? I can’t keep doing this pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tonight we’ll rest your stomach: nothing by mouth for now, hold the tube feeds, give IV fluids with dextrose to protect your blood sugar, and treat pain and nausea. We’ll continue your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If you stop my feeds, will my sugar crash even with the IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use dextrose-containing IV fluids and check your sugars every four hours. If we see them trending down, we can adjust quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think the tube is in the wrong place or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now there’s nothing suggesting it’s displaced—no leakage, no severe distention, and you’re still passing gas and stool. We’ll keep monitoring closely, and if anything changes we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs look reassuring—no major abnormalities that point to infection or pancreatitis. We’ll repeat labs as needed and keep an eye on hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also really anxious. Every time I’m here I feel like I’m stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll keep your home medications for anxiety and depression going, and we can also involve support services if you’d like.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after we held the tube feeds and started the dextrose IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain eased up some. Still there, but not as sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful information. Your blood sugars overnight stayed in a safe range, and you didn’t have symptoms of low sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So does that mean the feeds are causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests the pain may be triggered by feeding or by the tube itself—either the stomach being stimulated or the abdominal wall around the tube. It doesn’t mean anything dangerous is happening, but it guides our plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going to need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: At this point, no. We’re managing conservatively, and there’s no sign you need an operation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got a chest X-ray yesterday to make sure there wasn’t an infection in the lungs contributing to symptoms. It was clear—no pneumonia or fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just want to know why I keep ending up here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a complicated course after bariatric surgery and reversal, and you’re balancing two hard problems: protecting your stomach lining and managing hypoglycemia. We’re going to try to reduce reliance on tube feeds if it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’d like to start a careful trial of oral intake—small amounts, spaced out—while we continue to monitor sugars. How does your pain feel this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better than when I came in. I’m nervous to eat because it hurts when I try solids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start gently. The goal is to see if you can meet your needs by mouth without triggering pain or low sugars. We’ll keep nausea medicine available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If my sugar drops, what will I feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Common symptoms are shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, or feeling very hungry. If you feel any of those, call right away—we’ll check a fingerstick and treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been slowly weaning the dextrose IV. Your fingerstick sugars have stayed stable, mostly in the low 100s, and you’ve been asymptomatic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That surprises me. I thought I couldn’t go without the tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may be that with the right pattern of eating—small, frequent, low-glycemic carbs with protein—you can maintain safer sugars. We want to prove that safely here before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m not eating much. I don’t have an appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been tracking your intake with calorie counts, and you’re right—it’s been low. If it stays low, we’ll need a strategy to help you eat enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to talk about appetite. Since your intake has been poor, we’d like to start a medication called dronabinol—also known as Marinol—to stimulate appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with everything else I’m on? And will it make me feel weird?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start at a low dose and monitor you. Some people feel sleepy or a little off; if that happens, tell us and we can adjust. The goal is to help you take in enough calories by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you do after starting Marinol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually felt hungry for the first time in a while. I ate more yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your calorie count improved significantly, and your sugars stayed stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I can keep the tube off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re encouraged. We’ll keep the tube feeds held while we confirm you can consistently meet most of your needs by mouth and keep sugars safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is still there, but it’s less intense when the feeds aren’t running. Is that what you’re seeing too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pain pattern fits with that. We’re continuing your acid suppression and sucralfate, and using pain medication as needed while trying to avoid anything you’re allergic to like NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried I’ll go home and crash again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re building a plan you can follow at home: structured eating, glucose monitoring, and close follow-up. We’ll also make sure you have clear instructions on when to seek help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A specialist team is going to meet with you about managing hypoglycemia with diet—small frequent meals, low-glycemic carbs, and protein-focused snacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you explain low-glycemic in plain terms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means choosing carbs that don’t spike your blood sugar quickly—paired with protein. The goal is to avoid big swings: no rapid highs followed by lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your intake yesterday was close to 90% of your daily calorie goal—about 1400 to 1600 calories out of an 1800 calorie target. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think I could do that. The Marinol really helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your fingerstick sugars remain steady in the low 100s without symptoms. That’s exactly what we want to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m eating more, why do I still need the tube at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now it’s a safety net. The plan is not to remove it immediately. We want sustained stability at home first, then reassess in clinic. The long-term plan is to remove it in a few months if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’ve only needed the ondansetron once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Less nausea usually makes it easier to keep up with the small frequent meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still anxious at night. I keep thinking my sugar will drop while I’m asleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fear is common with your history. We’ll review a home monitoring plan: checking before bed, and checking more often if you feel symptoms. We also recommend using your Dexcom continuous glucose monitor to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to practice the discharge routine while you’re still here: meals and snacks spaced out, protein snacks, and glucose checks before meals and at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I’m about to drive and I’m not sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar before driving, and don’t drive if you feel symptoms. If it’s low, treat it and recheck. We’ll put that in your written instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. It’s not gone, but it’s not like when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s consistent with what we’ve seen: holding tube feeds reduced the pain, and you’ve been able to maintain nutrition by mouth with Marinol support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nurse said something about tube feeding again today. Are we restarting it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing a controlled reintroduction of nutrition through the tube today to make sure you can tolerate it if you ever need it as backup. We’ll watch your pain and sugars closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’ll flare the pain back up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it does, we’ll stop and reassess. The goal is to leave you with a safe plan—either oral-only if you’re stable, or a backup option if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did you feel with the tube nutrition trial this afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It didn’t go great at first, but it wasn’t unbearable. I’m still better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks—that helps us tailor the plan. We’ll keep focusing on oral intake as the main strategy, with the tube as backup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge day if everything stays stable. You’ve been afebrile, your vitals are stable, your labs have been reassuring, and your sugars have stayed steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m happy to go home, but I’m scared the pain will come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If the pain worsens, if you develop fever, redness or drainage at the tube site, persistent vomiting, or you can’t keep your sugars safe—those are reasons to call or come back. Otherwise, we’ll manage this outpatient with close follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What exactly do I need to do for the sugar plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small frequent meals with low-glycemic carbs, spaced out through the day; snacks should be protein without carbs. Check glucose before meals and at bedtime, and more often if you have symptoms or before driving. Use your Dexcom to watch trends.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube—are you taking it out now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. You’ll follow up with our surgery clinic in a few weeks to re-evaluate the tube. If you keep doing well, the plan is to remove it in several months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I stay on all my stomach meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—continue pantoprazole twice daily, ranitidine daily, and sucralfate four times daily as prescribed. Those help protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have acetaminophen liquid as needed and your oxycodone liquid as needed, and continue gabapentin. Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of your allergy and ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I can do that. I just want my life back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’ve made real progress this admission—less pain off feeds, better oral intake with Marinol, and stable sugars. We’ll support you closely after discharge.
